Packages

  • model — Domain classes: exercises, plan, profile, logs, reminders, enums
  • planner — Turns a goal into a 7-day plan
  • data — Saving to and loading from SharedPreferences as JSON
  • health — BMI, BMR, calories, water, protein
  • suggestions — Rule-based tips
  • tracking — Weekly stats and streaks
  • reminders — Daily alarms and notifications
  • tutorial — Fetching exercise tutorial videos
  • app / viewmodel / ui — App wiring, UI state and Compose screens

All 67 app types across 11 packages. Use + / − or Fit to zoom, and drag to move around.

The core objects of the app: exercises, the plan, the user profile, logs and reminders.

OOP in this part

  • Abstraction + multilevel inheritance: Exercise is abstract, and its subclasses are Strength, Cardio and Flexibility. HiitExercise extends CardioExercise, which is marked open because Kotlin classes are final by default.
  • Runtime polymorphism: each subclass overrides estimatedMinutes() and scaledFor(). HiitExercise.caloriesBurned() calls super and then adds a 15% afterburn bonus.
  • Covariant return types: StrengthExercise.scaledFor() returns StrengthExercise, not just Exercise. C++ allows the same thing in virtual overrides.
  • Encapsulation: every UserProfile setter calls require(...), and the constructor goes through those setters, so an invalid profile can never exist.
  • Composition vs aggregation: a WorkoutPlan owns its 7 WorkoutSessions (filled diamond). A session only refers to Exercise objects, which are shared from ExerciseLibrary (hollow diamond).
  • Interfaces: five types implement Describable, so one UI function, DescribableRow, can draw all of them.

How a fitness goal becomes a 7-day plan. This is the code behind your “Strategy and Factory” slide.

OOP in this part

  • Strategy: the PlanStrategy interface has one concrete class per FitnessGoal.
  • Template Method: BasePlanStrategy.buildPlan() is final and always does the same steps: get the schedule, scale each exercise to the level, then wrap it in a plan. Subclasses only fill in weeklySchedule() and planName. In C++ this is a non-virtual public method that calls a protected pure virtual one.
  • Factory: WorkoutPlanFactory.strategyFor(goal) is the when block. Callers get back a PlanStrategy and never name a concrete class.
  • protected helpers: day() and rest() are visible to subclasses only. They're shown with # in the diagram.

Storage hidden behind a generic interface, and one container that creates every shared object.

OOP in this part

  • Generics with a bound: Repository<T : Identifiable> works for any type that has an id. This is like a C++20 template constrained by a concept.
  • One class, two uses: PrefsRepository<T> stores both WorkoutLogs and Reminders. The type-specific JSON conversion is handed off to an injected JsonMapper<T>.
  • Dependency injection: AppContainer builds every shared object once. Its fields are typed as interfaces (Repository, ReminderScheduler), so an implementation can be swapped, for example with a fake in tests.
  • Single responsibility: model classes don't know how to save themselves. That job belongs to the mapper objects.

Calculated health numbers and a rule-based suggestion engine.

OOP in this part

  • Interface with a default method: HealthMetric.formatted() has a body. Some metrics override it and others inherit it, much like a virtual function with a base implementation.
  • Composition: DailyCaloriesMetric contains a BmrMetric and builds on its result instead of inheriting from it.
  • Rules as objects: SuggestionEngine holds a list of SuggestionRules. Each one returns a Suggestion or null. Adding a rule never changes the engine (open/closed principle). Because it's a fun interface, a rule can also be a lambda.
  • Object contract: Suggestion implements Comparable, so .sorted() orders suggestions by Priority. In C++ you'd overload operator<.

How the screens get their data, and how reminders reach Android.

OOP in this part

  • Observer: profile, logs and reminders are mutableStateOf. When one changes, Compose redraws every screen that reads it. plan, stats and suggestions are computed from them.
  • Encapsulation: screens can read the state but not change it directly (private set). Every change goes through a ViewModel method, which also updates storage and alarms.
  • Programming to an interface: the ViewModel depends on ReminderScheduler. Only AlarmReminderScheduler knows about Android's AlarmManager.
  • Inheriting from the framework: FitMateApplication, MainActivity, FitnessViewModel and the two receivers each extend an Android base class and override its callback, such as onCreate or onReceive.
